chunks: What happens when a LiPo is overcharged. The question: What happens when you overcharge the battery?
Overcharging means pushing a lithium cell above its 4. 2 volts limit, or forcing in more charge than it can store. A small overcharge mainly shortens its life.
A larger one makes gas and metal deposits, and heat. In the worst case the cell goes into thermal runaway, which means venting and fire.
So chargers and protection circuits are built in layers to prevent it.
Think of pumping up a bike tire. Past the right pressure, it gets stiff and wears out sooner. Keep pumping and it bulges. Keep going and it can burst.
A cell goes through similar stages, but with a nasty twist: the extra energy turns into heat inside the cell, and heat speeds up the damaging reactions, which make more heat.
The safe window ends sharply at 4. 2 volts.
The orange band just above is where life loss accelerates and where protection ICs usually trip; the red region is where gas, plating and runaway risk build up if the abuse continues.
Overvoltage: a cell voltage above its safe limit, above about 4. 2 volts for the usual cell ("LiPo cell voltage range and why").
Lithium plating: lithium metal forming on a full anode, which can grow spikes through the separator.
Gas generation: the electrolyte breaking down into gas, which makes a pouch swell. Thermal runaway: self-feeding heating, ending in venting and possibly fire.
Protection IC: a chip that opens a switch when voltage goes too high ("Why charging and monitoring ICs matter").
A cell is held at 4. 2 volts when full. Going to 4. 25 or 4. 3 volts mostly shortens its life. Say a charger keeps pushing 1 amps into a 2 Ah cell until the voltage is 4. 5 volts.
That is 4. 5 watts going into a cell weighing about 45 g, and with an assumed 1 J per gram per kelvin it would warm by about 0.
1 K per second, or 6 K per minute, before any cooling. A protection chip opens a switch at about 4. 25 to 4. 35 volts, long before that. That is the whole idea.
"Overcharging is pushing a cell above 4. 2 volts or past what the anode can hold. A little over mostly shortens life.
Further over, the electrolyte oxidizes and makes gas so the pouch swells, and extra lithium plates as metal on the anode, which can grow dendrites.
The energy has nowhere to go but heat, which speeds up the reactions, and eventually the separator melts, the cell shorts and thermal runaway starts.
It's prevented in layers: an accurate charger with termination and timer, per-cell monitoring, a protection IC at about 4. 3 volts, and fuses or vents."
